problem: Sim-to-real transfer methods for navigation and stationary manipulation do not address long-horizon mobile manipulation, which needs both perceptual generalization and compositional reuse of multiple skills. The prior EMBER (latent-dynamics MBRL) method fails in the real world on such tasks.
motivation: Real-world data covering the breadth and compositional variability of long-horizon mobile manipulation is infeasible to collect, so simulation training is attractive. The observation is that factorizing an activity into primitive visual skills, each RL-trained in a photorealistic, heavily randomized simulator, can transfer to a real robot.
key_idea: Factorize a long-horizon activity into primitive visuomotor skills, each learned in randomized photorealistic simulation with a success detector, Q-function and CEM planning, then recompose them at test time with a symbolic planner driven by the success detectors.
insight: Photorealism and domain randomization are both essential to sim-to-real transfer: removing photorealism drops cleaning_kitchen success from 53.3% to 0%, and halving randomization ranges drops it to 23.3%. Dropping the latent dynamics model (EMBER's MBOLD, and BEE's visual foresight) is also crucial, since both get 0/30 in the real world. Learned skills beat scripted ones (1/30).
method: Skill factorization and symbolic planning: the BEHAVIOR/BDDL symbolic goal is decomposed into K=5 skills (grasp, place, open, close, wipe); a symbolic planner picks the next skill from the goal and current symbolic state until the goal is met.

Success detectors as state grounding: per-skill learned detectors classify latent image encodings, giving a binary per-skill reward, detecting skill completion, and mapping raw pixels to the symbolic state.
Per-skill VAE: each skill has its own VAE that compresses 112x112 images into latents used by the detectors and Q-functions (EMBER shares one VAE across skills).
Q-learning with CEM: Q-functions are trained from the binary rewards (target maximized over 200 sampled actions), and actions are chosen with CEM over Q-values; no latent dynamics model is used.
Extra object-aware inputs: an 'in-view image' and a 'masked image' of the target object tell the policy which camera sees the object.

Photorealism and 14-dimension domain randomization: photorealistic iGibson rendering with randomization of objects, textures, lighting, robot placement, cameras, scenes, physics and robot arm textures.
Action interface: small pose deltas of the two end-effectors (6D) and base (3D), plus head, torso and gripper joint positions.

setting.backbone: Per-skill VAE + success detectors + Q-functions (trained from scratch with RL in simulation), symbolic planner for composition
setting.training_data: RL trajectories collected in photorealistic, domain-randomized iGibson kitchen simulation; no real data (scale not given)
setting.observation: N RGB cameras at 112x112 (3Hz) plus 19 joint angles (proprioception); 360° 2D LiDAR used only as a fail-safe, not visible to the learner
setting.action_space: continuous small pose changes of two end-effectors (6D) and base (3D), plus head/torso/gripper joint positions
setting.privileged: none (a symbolic goal from BEHAVIOR/BDDL is specified by a human; a real kitchen is used for validation)

numbers.eval_set_note: 30 real-world trials (10 in each of 3 kitchens)

results: M-EMBER completes real-world cleaning_kitchen in 16/30 trials (53.3%), versus 1/30 for scripted skills and 0/30 for EMBER and BEE. Removing photorealism drops it to 0/30, and halving randomization to 7/30.
limitations: Success rate is still low (53%), the domain gap remains large, and only one activity in three kitchens was tested
Uses RGB only and cannot take depth input; failures include collisions, leftover objects, and failed grasps
Baseline comparisons are limited (no Habitat rearrangement baselines) and the related-work claims are not empirically validated
